Mr. Speaker, on Friday the hon.

I have not had an opportunity to read the article in the Winnipeg Free Press but I have read the Canadian Press dispatch. subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF GOVERNMENT POLICY ON CONTINENTAL SHELF
speechtext: should like to direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs to whom I sent notice. Has Canada made any submission to or given consideration to the minutes of the United Nations' law committee on high seas matters with respect to the continental shelf? Will the minister inform the house as to the government's policy with respect to the continental shelf?

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secrelary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF GOVERNMENT POLICY ON CONTINENTAL SHELF
speechtext:
With reference to the first part of the question, the hon. member is referring, I think, to the recent debate in the legal committee of the United Nations general assembly which has been considering the report of the international law commission on the work of its fifth session, as I

recall it, on the continental shelf. The government has been following this debate in the United Nations closely, and on November 24 last the Canadian representative on this committee, the hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. Macnaughton), made a statement of the preliminary views of the Canadian government. I can make that statement available to the hon. member. The report, that is the international law commission report, was not received until shortly before the general assembly opened. For this and other reasons the sixth committee resolved to withhold final consideration of the draft articles on the continental shelf until the commission had completed its work on the regime of the high seas.
As far as the second part of the question is concerned, the Canadian government has sought to relate Canada's action on this matter to the opinions and actions of other countries, more particularly since the doctrine of the continental shelf is a new departure in international law for which few, if any, precedents exist.
The house will recall that a special committee has been studying the question of territorial waters. The doctrine of the continental shelf is closely related to the deliberations of this committee, which is now awaiting an opinion by an outside legal expert. The government would prefer therefore to withhold further comment until this opinion has been received and considered.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Before we get down to the business of the day, I think some comment should be made on the beautiful decorations on our desks. I have inquired and I am told that they have been placed here by the hon. members for Hamilton East (Mr. Ross) and Hamilton South (Mr. Reinke) in honour of the victory of the Hamilton Tiger Cats. I think it is a beautiful gesture, and the effect on the eye as one comes into the house is wonderful.
492	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Schneider
In the first place I wish to associate myself with those who have offered their congratulations to you, Mr. Speaker, on your well-deserved promotion, and also to the Deputy Speaker on his promotion. I wish to extend my congratulations to the mover (Mr. Hollingworth) and seconder (Mr. Vil-leneuve) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. They did a magnificent job.
As a comparatively new member of this house I shall confine my remarks almost entirely to the affairs of the constituency which sent me here. My first duty is to my riding. Many people have spoken to me about a matter of which I had not heard previously, namely, the possibility of granting half-fare rate to our service personnel as they travel on the railways. I have made inquiries and I find there are some privileges granted to the personnel who travel on leave. They are granted two and one-half cents per mile when they travel over and above 500 miles. The government is not really hurting themselves in making a grant like that. Besides, that is allowed only in the case of annual leave.
On embarkation leave these men are provided with full transportation charges, their pullman and meals. But that is no more than right. I would draw your attention to the fact that sometimes men are stationed at great distances from their homes. They have no control over where they are stationed and they may be almost the width of the continent away from their families. A man may receive a call that his wife or a child is sick and I understand that if he goes home under those circumstances he must pay his full fare. I do not think that is right. I remember in the first and second great wars army personnel were granted half-fare privileges and I would appeal to the government and the authorities to consider the granting of halffare transportation to our personnel when they travel other than in the two instances I have cited.
I think this would give more encouragement to young men to go into the active service. We are spending a lot of money on advertising and then we find that the men who enlist are given a deal like that. They certainly are not overpaid and I think such a privilege would be a welcome thing to the boys in the armed services.
During the last session I made a plea along with others to the Department of National Health and Welfare that the means test on blind allowances be eliminated. There has been a lot of discussion on this question since and the matter has been mentioned on the

floor of this house by many hon. members. I think it would be a popular move. These handicapped people do not have the same opportunities for recreation as do sighted people and perhaps they would be inclined to work a few more hours if they were not penalized. If we cannot eliminate the means test we should at least increase the allowable income.	[DOT]
At the present time the allowable income in the case of a blind single man is $840. After he has earned $840 his blind allowance is affected. A sighted single person has an allowable income of $1,000 per year. In the case of a blind married man, the allowable income is $1,320 whereas the sighted person has an allowable income of $2,000. It would be no more than fair to raise the allowable incomes for blind persons to those paid to sighted persons, and I ask for that at least.
In my maiden speech last year I spoke of the glories of Waterloo North and there is no need to go into them again. I would remind the house that Waterloo North is a highly industrialized community and the first requisite of happy people is steady employment. Fortunately this steady employment has been assured by most of the factories in our district, but there are two which have been in difficulty for a long time.
I do not feel it is proper, on the floor of the house, to raise questions of tariffs and dumping, but I would advise hon. members that the difficulties facing these factories have been under consideration for a good many years. This problem is one of those things that have always been with us. These two plants have deteriorated and their operations have been decreased steadily over the years. I ask permission to present these matters on the floor of the house.
The first matter has reference to barrels. There is a large barrel factory in Waterloo, one of the few remaining tight-cooperage plants in the country. It is not everyone who has the skill to make a tight barrel. Of the five cooperage plants in Canada, two are still operating as cooperage shops but I believe only the one in Waterloo is active. It is hard to see people who have spent their lives at this skilled trade being laid off.
The reason for the reduction in the volume of business done by this plant is that our government allows the importation of 25,000 barrels per month. These barrels are purchased at from 15 to 25 cents apiece. They can be bought at that price because they have been used once, but in my opinion they are even better than new barrels. Most of these barrels have been used for the maturing of bonded whisky in the United States. They are available there because under the pure food

laws of that country they cannot be used the second time, even for the maturing of whisky.
This is a clear case of dumping. The cost of production in the United States, I am told, is about the same as in Canada, about $25 a barrel. If this practice continues we will not have a cooperage plant left in Canada. If something should happen it may be that the United States could not ship barrels to us any more and we would be left without a cooperage plant and without men who could make tight barrels. In an emergency that might prove to be a very serious thing.
The customs department has made one concession in that they have placed on these barrels a nominal value for duty purposes of $3. That means that the importer pays about 60 cents per barrel duty. When he buys the barrel for 25 cents his cost is only 85 cents for an excellent barrel which would cost $25 to make.
I do not want to complain about this without suggesting a remedy. None of my people are asking for higher tariffs or higher duty. We all agree that duties are high enough. Our problem is the valuation under which these articles come in. Section 35 of the Customs Act defines valuation for duty as the fair market value. This problem could be settled by defining the fair market value as a reasonable advance over manufacturing costs, including selling and administrative costs plus a fair profit. If that definition could be placed in section 35 instead of simply saying fair market value, then our people would be well satisfied. I urge the Department of National Revenue to make this change in order that one of our oldest and steadiest industries may survive. There would be no conflict under the act with GATT-that is, the general agreement on tariffs and trade. This or a similar definition of fair market value will solve another problem in my district, which is the problem of plastic buttons. When I go into the Department of National Revenue they smile because they know this problem has been inherited by me from my two predecessors. The production of buttons has been going down in volume for years because of the importation of American buttons which, manufacturers claim, are put on the market here at costs below those of Canadian production.
The department has been very co-operative and has even sent a man down to the United States to check on the claim that these buttons are not being dumped here, and that they comply with the law in all respects. They attempted to ascertain whether the sales price was equal in the United States to the price being charged in Canada. If we apply the same definition to buttons as
The Address-Mr. Schneider I asked for in the case of barrels I would say that this problem would be solved. The tariff on buttons is about 25 per cent and I think that is plenty. It hurts to see these lifetime employees thrown out of employment because of unfair importations.
Here is a telegram I received yesterday from one of our rubber footwear manufacturers in Kitchener. He urges the government to consider the problem of foreign canvas shoes the importation of which is threatening the Canadian footwear industry. Most imports, he states, are from Hong Kong and India where labour rates are reported as 30 cents per day. Imports of canvas footwear are now at 25 per cent of total Canadian consumption. Canadian industry cannot begin to meet low prices caused by cheap labour rates, he said.
Thirty cents a day, against in this country up to $1.40 an hour. It is impossible to compete with that. Here again I would say that all we want is a fair valuation on products coming into Canada. I quote from the Kitchener-Waterloo Record which gives the comments of several manufacturers in Kitchener. One states in this article dated November 26, 1953:
Importations which harm basic Canadian industry must be carefully studied. I strongly urge the government to thoroughly investigate all steps which could be taken to protect the Canadian manufacturers and labour forces.
Another one states:
When these imports are considered in terms of dollar value the situation becomes even more serious. The future of the Canadian industry is in a serious position. This same trouble was beginning just before the war, but it stopped when hostilities began . . .
At present such a low valuation is put on the low-cost footwear that the import duty is negligible . . .
There is one further comment:
The government could put a higher valuation on the product, thus causing a higher duty to be charged when it is brought into the country.
I make this plea on behalf of my people in the Kitchener district. We ask that a proper valuation be put on these goods. We do not ask for higher tariffs.
In closing I want to make one comment on a question which has been raised many times since this present session opened, and that is the loss of foreign trade. My own company is very deeply interested in foreign trade. We sent as many as seven carloads of meat per week to England before the difficulties began, but today we do not send one, with the possible exception of quantities contained in food parcels. I am very much concerned personally about this foreign trade and I would like to warn the house about the seriousness of the situation. This is a situation which no one has mentioned with the

The Address-Mr. Churchill exception of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). The statement he made is true, namely, that we have priced ourselves out of world markets. We have pushed the prices so high that we have a high degree of prosperity here but in doing so the result has been that we have lost our markets abroad.
I want to draw this to the attention of hon. members. They should keep in mind that they have pleaded and begged and criticized regarding prices being too low while at the same time the prices prevailing in Canada have been the highest in the world.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Deputy Speaker, may I first join with others who have already spoken in this debate in expressing my congratulations to you and to the Speaker. I think the opinion is generally held that the rules, customs and traditions of this house are in safe keeping in your hands and in those of the Speaker himself.
Last Friday the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) expressed great surprise that no one up to that time had mentioned the subject of national defence. That, I consider, was an invitation to hon. members to enter this debate. I thought the general plan at this session was to curtail this particular debate but when a number of cabinet ministers enter it then obviously others will join in.
I had no intention of participating at this particular point in our proceedings but I would not like the Minister of National Defence to think that I am unappreciative of the opportunity that he has afforded. I regret his unavoidable absence because I do not like to offer advice to him when he cannot be here. On the other hand I have to take this opportunity.
Yesterday the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Pearkes) dealt in his usual able manner with the general defence plans. I propose to confine myself to the army. However, first I wonder if it would be possible to clear up some problems in connection with the use of the words found on page 358 of Hansard, in the second column. The minister, speaking of the conflict in Korea, used the word "war" three times and the word "aggression" four times. The word "aggression", which the dictionary defines simply as quarrel, has acquired an enlarged meaning during the last few years. It appears to be a substitute for "war" or to mean "invasion or attack" or to mean something a little less than war and therefore not as serious or as important. Sometimes the watering-down process is carried further and the expression "police action" is used. That seems to me to be somewhat ridiculous.

There was a war in Korea, one of the bloodiest and the most costly in the history of the world. Millions of men died or were wounded in warfare in Korea. Our own Canadian casualties were heavy enough. When one considers that Canadian troops in relatively small numbers were in Korea for about two and one-half years and that at no time was the 25th brigade engaged in a major battle as a brigade but at battalion or company strength, a casualty list of 1,558 represents 85 per cent of the front line fighting strength of three infantry battalions. It shows the serious nature of the patrol actions and the various engagements in which our troops participated. Surely it is no compliment and no mark of respect to these gallant men to term the war in which they were engaged an "aggression" or a "police action". I have no doubt that they underwent as much hardship and encountered as much danger as any Canadians in other wars in which our country has been engaged. War was hell in General Sherman's time. It always has been and always will be, and the Korean war was no exception. Let us call it by its right name. In addition to confusing us with regard to what the Korean war should be called, the minister has endeavoured to write history. He used these words, and I quote from Hansard, page 358:
This was the first time, I believe, in the history of the world that 16 nations, . . . joined together in armed action to stop aggression. It was the first time that nations had acted together in peace as an international force . . .
The minister is doubtless right in saying that this was the first time that as many as 16 nations supplied armed forces to an army operating in one theatre; but I did not realize that this had been done in time of peace. I thought that war broke out in June, 1950, when the North Korean army invaded South Korea and that the 16 nations joined together to fight that war.
Then there are three other sentences on the same page to which I should like to make reference. They are as follows:
The objective was not victory. The objective was to prevent aggression by stopping aggression.
For that reason at times the war and its results have not appeared spectacular; nonetheless the objective was just as great a one as the objective of victory in a war, and the objective was achieved just as definitely from the military point of view as it could have been had victory been achieved in a war.
What all that means I do not know. I thought that the objective was to drive the invaders out of South Korea, that that was achieved by warfare and that victory was gained to that extent. A great many wars have ended in exactly the same way, by a country expelling an invader.

In connection with our contribution to NATO the minister mentioned the 27th brigade and used what seems to me to be extravagant language. These are his words, and again I quote him:
. . . that brigade in its training, record and exercises made a reputation for military competency which I do not think has ever been matched . . . by any Canadian forces.
A great deal of unfavourable criticism has been directed at the 27th brigade. I have no intention of entering into the merits of that criticism, except to say that such unfavourable criticism is regrettable and must have been damaging to morale. However, I think that if more information about many things was made available here in the House of Commons there would be less need for members or other people to be dependent upon press reports for their knowledge of events and less need for correspondents to feel compelled to raise such issues. In view of the arrangements that were made subsequently for educational courses for the 27th brigade and for an extension of privileges to the troops, and for other matters, it would appear that there was some justification for some of the criticism. However, I think the minister is now going to the other extreme in declaring that the 27th brigade made a reputation for military competency never matched by any Canadian forces. No brigade ever reaches a satisfactory state of military competency until it has been tested in battle. The 27th brigade was never tested in battle, and that is something for which we may all be very thankful. Is the minister suggesting that the brigades of the Canadian corps in the first war and of the 1st Canadian army in the second war and of the Korean force who trained for a longer period than did the 27th brigade, and who were more thoroughly tested in battle, were not superior to this brigade whose service was wholly under conditions of peace?
Consider also the turnover in manpower of the 27th brigade. After only one year overseas 1,900 men of that brigade were returned to Canada and replaced by recruits. In the period 1952-53 fully one-third of the brigade was replaced. Under these conditions it would be extraordinarily difficult to keep a brigade at a high state of efficiency. Whatever the minister may now say in extravagant terms of the 27th brigade, whatever inspired testimonials he may be able to produce, the fact remains that the 27th brigade suffered from the beginning from a serious handicap for which the officers and the men were in no way responsible. The policy adopted for the formation of that brigade was unsound. For
The Address-Mr. Churchill that policy the minister must be held responsible. If that policy has been changed-and I believe it has been changed-the minister should so inform the house.
The policy to which I refer was, of course, the forming of composite battalions drawn from a large number of reserve units, with the separate companies of each battalion being permitted to retain and to wear the insignia of the parent reserve unit. My sympathy from the start was with the battalion commanders who were faced with a most difficult situation. I have twice been through a similar experience and am perfectly familiar with the problems involved. You cannot begin to develop unity within a battalion or commence to build up esprit de corps until all the officers and the men of a battalion are wearing the same cap badge and the same shoulder flash. In reading the debate of May, 1951, on this subject, I noticed that the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) warned the minister that his plan was unwise, but the warning went unheeded. Hence from the start the 27th brigade was compelled to operate under a handicap. That they managed as well as they did stands to their credit. They deserve praise and they deserve our thanks.
I should now like to offer some criticism concerning the make-up of the Canadian army. The suggestions are not new but repetition seems to be essential in this house, for the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) has not yet acted in this matter. I have two complaints to make. The first one is that our Canadian army as a whole- and I underline that phrase-although highly trained in many respects is not fully modern, and is not up to the standard of other armies. It is out of balance. This results mainly from the failure to develop our armoured formations. In the three years of the Korean war and in the two years of providing a NATO force in Europe we have utilized only two squadrons of armour. The Canadian armoured corps is not being developed. Yet in the second world war armour played a dominant role; and in the present armies of the great powers, armoured formations are receiving very great attention.
Tank regiments have a mobility that cannot be matched by infantry. They have greater fire power. They require fewer men and they are effective in saving lives. Sufficient proof that tanks save lives is available. Why is armour neglected in the Canadian army? What are we doing with respect to developing specialized armoured equipment such as that which was used so effectively by the 79th British armoured division in northwest

The Address-Mr. Churchill Europe? The success of the Normandy landing and of the campaign in northwest Europe was due in large measure to the employment of ordinary tanks and to the employment of the special tanks of the 79th division. Is this lesson of that war to be forgotten?
My second complaint is allied to the first. Both concern the saving of the lives of our soldiers. Two years ago I spoke in this house concerning the employment of the armoured personnel carrier for infantry and advocated that type of vehicle for use in the equipping and training of a Canadian army. Subsequently, along with others, I supported the view that an armoured force in Europe would be more suitable than an infantry brigade and that if infantry were employed there, they should have armoured carriers. My remarks on armoured carriers received no attention. I return to this subject because I consider it to be of the greatest importance. It is of the greatest importance because the armoured carrier is the best device yet discovered to save the lives of infantrymen. Now that the program of defence preparedness has reached an advanced stage, I urge the minister to give some attention to the problem of how to reduce casualties among the infantry under battle conditions. Preparations for this should be made in time of peace. I am surprised and disappointed that this problem has received such little attention.
The armoured personnel carrier was devised by Canadians and brought to a high state of efficient use by Canadians. Yet the Canadian army has either discarded it entirely or put it into mothballs. Will the minister give an answer concerning this neglect of the best life-saving device ever developed for infantry? Consider for a moment the great strides that have been made by the air force during the last thirty years in devising ways and means of protecting the lives of pilots and aircrew. The parachute was not in use by airmen in the first world war. It is now standard equipment. Special armoured protection has been introduced into cockpits. In some planes a catapulting device may be used to eject a pilot in danger of crashing. The navy has never been neglectful of protective armour plating when possible, and of life-saving equipment for the men who go down to the sea in ships.
But what of the infantry who are called upon to bear the brunt of the fighting on the battlefield? If the Canadian brigade now in Europe should be called upon to go into battle next week or next year and has to make an attack, the infantrymen will advance

in the very same way and with precisely the same lack of protection as the infantry in the 1914 to 1918 war and as most of the infantry in the second world war. But in the last nine months of the campaign in northwest Europe a new method was found and used effectively to take infantry from the assembly area and start line right into the enemy's position with protection such as the infantry had never had before against enemy machine guns, mortars and shellfire.
Nor did this lessen the effectiveness of the infantry. On the contrary, it increased their fighting efficiency for they arrived at their objective unwearied by a long and toilsome march. They were able to take forward larger supplies of ammunition and they achieved tactical surprise. Why has this lesson of the war been neglected? Why has this type of protection for our infantry not been made available? How much evidence is required? I gave some of it two years ago. Armoured personnel carriers used by Canadians were involved in at least sixty actions from the battle of Falaise to the end of the war. They took at least fifty-four infantry battalions into battle. They operated under all manner of conditions in actual battle, attacks by day and by night, attacks in good weather and in rain and snow, attacks on icy roads and in mud, and in all these operations the casualties to the infantry were less than for any other attacks undertaken by infantry.
It is in that last difficult phase moving from the start line to the objective that infantry casualties are so heavy, and it is in that phase that the armoured carrier provides protection. I hope that the minister will investigate this problem himself. What worthier achievement for a minister of national defence than to provide suitable protection for those who suffer the heaviest casualties in wartime? I do not ask the minister to take my word for this. I would suggest to him a course of investigation.
The minister is not unaware of the heavy toll of casualties in the fighting in Normandy in 1944. Does he know why that casualty list was so great? Does he know why the infantry had difficulty in reaching Carpiquet airfield, to use only one example of that period, although Canadian tanks were already established on that objective? Is he familiar with the method by which infantry were carried forward and kept close to the tanks in the opening phase of the Falaise battle? I suggest that he examine the record of these actions.
Then I would direct his attention to three engagements that are useful for purposes of

comparison. I can give other examples, but let him examine the attack conducted under the direction of the third British division on Wunssum Wood in January, 1945. He will be interested to learn that in that attack undertaken in battalion strength over a wide expanse of open country, not one single infantry casualty occurred until the enemy position was reached. He may then examine the details of the attack under the direction of the 43rd British division on the town of Putt in Germany in January, 1945. That was a battalion attack across a wide expanse of open country. No infantry casualty was sustained until the German position was reached. Let him contrast these two operations with the Canadian attack on the town of Udem in Germany in front of the Hochwald forest in the spring of 1945. That was a brigade effort across a 1,400 yard expanse of open country. Heavy casualties were suffered by the infantry as they made their way across that open stretch of country swept with enemy fire.
In the first two examples that I have given the infantry were carried forward under the protection of armoured carriers. In the Canadian attack on Udem no armoured carriers were used although armoured carriers had been in use in northwest Europe since the preceding August. I am asking the minister to make his own investigation of this problem concerning protection for our infantry. I do not know with whom he may consult. He may limit his discussion to his generals and staff officers. It is with no disrespect to these distinguished gentlemen that I suggest he also consult those who had firsthand experience of armoured carriers in action. I refer to infantry officers who had actual experience of armoured personnel carriers, and to squadron commanders of the first Canadian armoured carrier regiment. He might further consider what is being done with armoured carriers in the American and British armies, and then do better. The Americans had no experience with armoured personnel carriers in the campaign in northwest Europe except when they borrowed them from the British during the counterattack by the Germans in the Ardennes.
The vehicle that they have designed for use as an infantry carrier, if my information concerning it is correct, is in my opinion unsuitable. The British infantry carrier, of which I have some information, is also in my opinion unsuitable. Canada led the way in the development of the armoured infantry carrier and can regain that lead if attention is paid to the problem.
The minister has arranged a series of visits for members of parliament to various depots, camps and training establishments. This is
The Address-Mr. Bruneau all very good in its way. It will show the complexity and the difficulties of the problem in preparing the groundwork for our armed services, preparing the infrastructure, which is a term that the minister sometimes uses. But when you have seen one depot you have seen them all; when you have seen one military camp or one radar station or one training establishment you have seen them all. I have no objection to the plan of providing comfortable quarters for our servicemen or plenty of amenities, but the objective of all this preparation, the objective of all our immense expenditures is to produce an effective fighting machine. The demonstration which the minister should put on for hon. members, and which I think he cannot put on, is of an entirely different nature.
The minister at this stage in our preparations should be able to assemble a brigade of tanks, with a brigade of infantry in armoured carriers, supported by self-propelled, fully tracked artillery, and with ammunition and supplies brought forward in fully tracked vehicles, or supplied by air. I suggest that the minister should cancel his proposed junkets to base establishments and that, instead, he should put on a demonstration that will show whether our army as a whole is a modern, mechanized force, or is just a replica of the first world war organization, when the frail human body was pitted against murderous steel.
In conclusion, these are questions which I put to the minister: Why is the Canadian army as a whole not being brought up to the standard required in modern warfare? Why is the armoured corps not being enlarged and utilized in strength? And, most important of all, why is not armoured protection for our infantry being provided?
We cannot evade these issues merely by hoping that war will not occur. We cannot evade these issues by presuming that warfare will be entirely changed by some new weapons of destruction. We certainly should not neglect the useful lessons learned in warfare. My charge is that we are neglecting the most useful lesson learned in actual battle conditions for the protection of the lives of the infantry.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the mover (Mr. Hollingworth) and the seconder (Mr. Villeneuve) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. The way in which they performed this arduous task commends them to our attention.
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, may I be allowed, on behalf of those whom I have the honour to represent in this house and of those who have preceded

The Address-Mr. Bruneau me on this floor, to congratulate you and to pay you a most sincere tribute on the occasion of your election to the high post which you now occupy; this is an honour you have deserved because of your fine spirit of industry, justice and equity. I am convinced that, whatever their political persuasion, all members will find in you the champion and the defender of their rights and privileges.
(Text):
Mr. Speaker, as the first representative of the new constituency of Glengarry-Pres-cott, neighbouring that of Vaudreuil-Sou-langes, I wish to say to the house that the people I represent, and the people in the last-named constituency, have always practised a good-neighbour policy, and I am sure will continue to do so for a good many years to come.
Following the last redistribution the historical constituencies of Glengarry and Prescott were merged, and this riding extends now from a point a very few miles from Cornwall to the border of the province of Quebec at Point Fortune, and from Dalhousie Mills on the Soulanges canal to a point twenty miles from Ottawa. Geographically, no other riding in the country enjoys greater advantages. Halfway between the metropolis of Montreal and Ottawa, the capital city of Canada, Glengarry-Prescott constitutes the whole tip of eastern Ontario, halfway between the St. Lawrence and the Ottawa rivers. Highways 17, 2 and 34 pass through this whole territory, as well as highway No. 8, Which is just across the river in the province of Quebec.
For over a century people of English, Scottish, Irish and French extraction and of all religious denominations have lived together in peace, harmony and bonne entente, helping each other, enjoying the same happiness and sharing the same bereavements.
Hand in hand, the people of Glengarry-Prescott worked together and colonized the whole eastern tip of Ontario where today is found the richest farm land in what is known as the golden triangle, in the Ottawa and St. Lawrence valley.
The people I represent hope that, in the not too distant future, the channelling of the St. Lawrence seaway will materialize, thus developing more hydro power which will give to that forgotten section of the province the prosperity it can rightly expect from undreamed of possibilities. We sincerely hope that, with decentralization of industry, thriving municipalities in our region will have their share of small industry.
It has been repeated time and time again in the house that industry agglomerated

today in the main cities of Canada would become an easy target for an enemy power should there be an attack by air. Moreover, with our immense territory extending over half a continent, there is no reason why our population should be settled mainly around four or five large cities. Such a decentralization would bring about a better balance of population and distribution of earning power.
Economic and strategic reasons make such decentralization increasingly imperative. Decentralization relieves transport congestion in heavily populated areas and facilitates the quick movement of traffic in times of both peace and war. New methods of air warfare along with the shortening of distances are undoubtedly the most compelling reasons for this decentralization.
There is in my riding, sir, ample power for the operation of almost any type of industry. The county is well endowed with rail and highway transportation facilities. We have thriving municipalities, which undoubtedly could offer great advantages for operation of industry.
True, our main industry is agriculture; but municipalities as such cannot rely solely upon it, and the item in the speech from the throne, where mention is made of bills to amend the Municipal Grants Act, will, I am sure, or should be implemented in such a way as to allow municipal corporations to go out and invite industrialists to set up shop within their walls. The full development of Canada's agricultural possibilities is also an essential consideration.
Glengarry-Prescott is basically a rural riding and ranks as the largest cheese-producing area in the British commonwealth. It has a yearly output of over 6,835,519 pounds of cheese from 61 cheese factories in operation. The people I represent rely upon the manufacture of this commodity for an income which is a very important factor in its economy; and, to that end, I strongly urge the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) to do his utmost to see that the support price is maintained at a level of not less than 30 to 32 cents a pound for Cheddar cheese. I hope that this spring we will not see a recurrence of a drop in the price of cheese such as that with which the farming element in my constituency had to cope last spring. In the same way, our agricultural class is at present also concerned over the price of beef and pork.
I say here, as I have on many previous occasions, that we certainly have no objections to subsidies granted to the western farmers, but we expect proportionately our

share of grants to farmers in eastern Canada, particularly those of the dairy industry centred mainly in this part of Canada.
Canadians throughout the country are in dire need of living accommodation at low cost and people with small incomes are unable to pay high rents for inadequate quarters. We will be asked to consider measures to increase and broaden the supply of mortgage money so that more people with moderate incomes will be able to find facilities to assist them to build their own homes. With our present world in turmoil and unrest, one of the greatest stabilizing factors could be homes owned by Canadian citizens.
The strength of a nation depends a good deal upon the security of its inhabitants. Home owners are a great asset to any government because they enjoy a form of security for the preservation of which they are willing to undergo great sacrifices. A national housing policy would be beneficial not 'only to individuals but to the nation at large, because it would be one of the best weapons to combat communism.
We all want, I am sure, to see new homes spreading throughout Canada and I hope methods will be implemented by which prospective owners will find themselves in a position where they can build their homes. But we shall have to make sure that the initial payment, which becomes a condition of ownership, is not too high for the average income earner. True, we grant a certain percentage of loan, but the difference is yet too high, I believe, to allow young couples to secure that ready cash enabling them to make use of this scheme.
I have the honour, sir, to represent in this house a riding that is made up of people of different nationalities and religious denominations who live together in harmony and bonne entente. Among them exist the most cordial and sympathetic relations. We understand each other and never stop to think of one as being Irish, Scottish or French. We consider one another as Canadians with the same interests and aspirations, kindled by the same love for the country. Now, how much closer would those ties and bonds of harmony be if we could look to the same symbol of harmony and unity, a truly Canadian flag behind which we could all rally, a flag which we could revere and love, for which we could fight and die?
Canada now ranks among the great nations of the world, and I believe that it is our duty to give our people a true symbol of Cana-dianism. I hope that during this session a measure will be brought into this house
The Address-Mr. Bruneau giving our people a Canadian flag which they can consider their own and acknowledge as their own.
When we initiate a study to improve social welfare, particularly the rehabilitation of disabled persons, to be implemented with the provinces, and a measure to facilitate the establishment throughout the country of invalidity assistance-though we already have such assistance in my province-I find that if some increase could be brought about in old age and invalidity assistance it would prove of tremendous relief to those people.
Now, there is one question that is of particular interest to me, Mr. Speaker, and that is help and encouragement to youth in this country. I feel that we have, in Canada, young people with talent, initiative and tremendous possibilities, but unfortunately they lack the means to put to some use these potentialities. With the eventual implementation of the recommendations of the Massey commission on the arts, letters and sciences why could we not devise some means whereby our young people could be given a helping hand and afforded the opportunity to better serve the country in a fashion more appropriate to their liking? I have seen a lot of young people come out of school with flying colours. They were brilliant in their studies and yet they are out looking for a job. They seek employment but truly if given the opportunity they would go into a field for which they feel they are better suited.
If our young people felt that there was a federal youth department where they could apply for assistance or guidance, I am sure that before too long we would have the experts that today we are seeking in other lands. This youth department on a national scale would certainly not infringe upon the provincial departments of education, but, in co-operation with those departments, we could have at the disposal of our young people experts in the different fields of learning, knowledge and craftsmanship who could interview our young people who have not yet gone out on their own in the struggle for life. These young people would be in a position to discuss with men of experience their own problems and aspirations. In all departments of this government we certainly have fields or divisions where these young people could ideally serve in all walks of life, we could make guidance available to the young men from the farm who could study, at the experimental farm or experimental stations throughout the country, the best ways of cultivation, new methods of farming that would improve the lot of those living on the homestead. Young people in industry could, under the supervision of this new department, learn for themselves and put
500	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Castleden to some use their own talents in order to best serve it, thus making our world a better place to live in.
The same applies to the different field of knowledge where, under the proper guidance and with the help of grants, our young people could follow a course best adapted to their aptitudes, in different universities. If we should help the young men of today it would, I am sure, pay dividends a hundredfold and give us better citizens for tomorrow. I hope, Mr. Speaker, that before too long Canada will have its own youth department which would pay countless dividends, and if we willingly spend billions to teach man to kill man, I believe the idea is worth considering and some effort should be made to help our young people better to serve this country.
Since the cease-fire in Korea, we have had peace pourparlers. Let us hope that those who have fallen on the hills of that corner of Asia have not done so in vain.
We hope, I am sure, sir, that we are entering an era of peace, prosperity and happiness and that it will be possible to divert our energies towards making this world not only a safer place to live in but a happier one, where everybody will be in a position, each in his own way, to serve, not only to maintain peace but to bring sunshine into the life of everyone.

speechtext:
The flood of congratulations from every part of the house and the sincere and high regard in which the Speaker is held by all are, I am sure, greatly appreciated by the Speaker himself. The opposition is particularly sensitive to the rulings of the Chair, and we have been very pleased to note the impartial justice and tolerance with which you, sir, have interpreted the rules in this house. They are a part, an essential part, of all British parliamentary procedure. You will, I am sure, continue to enjoy the respect of both sides of the house so long as you are in office.
Hon. members are elected to this house to speak for their constituencies and the people who sent them here. The people in my constituency sent me here to speak for them. It is a humbling responsibility and I can only hope that I shall be able to discharge it adequately.
In my opinion there are two features of Canadian life today which deserve the special consideration of all Canadian people. No. 1: I believe that blind allegiance to any political party by large masses of the people may be dangerous to democracy. No. 2: We in Canada should guard jealously our independence and our own kind of political democracy
[Mr. Bruneau.l

from the natural dangers of sharing a continent with a giant. We could become most dangerously dependent upon that nation.
With regard to my own constituency and that part of the west from which I come, I hasten on this my first opportunity to present some of the particular difficulties which are facing the people of Yorkton. However, before I do that I should like to convey to the government, particularly to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters), the appreciation of Yorkton for the fine public building built there last summer, costing almost $1 million. My presence here must not be interpreted as an indication that they do not appreciate that building. They do appreciate it deeply. It was something that was needed. The people of Yorkton and the constituency know that the continued welfare of that county and city depends to a large extent, or almost entirely, upon the prosperity of the farmers who live and produce in the northeastern part of the province of Saskatchewan.
Today that prosperity is in grave danger. Already there are signs of an economic setback, largely due to the lack of cash on the part of farmers from the sale of their 1953 crop. The ministers here appear to be unaware of the seriousness of the situation. I should like to draw to their attention the fact that in spite of the money that has been paid out in the province this year the costs of bringing in a crop are higher than they have ever been in the history of the west. The money which the farmers receive this year is in payment for their 1952 crop and the production costs of the 1953 crop are largely as yet unpaid.
Because of high costs farmers in the west are compelled to operate on credit and that credit is still on the books of the oil dealer, the machinery man, the grocer, the garage, the repairman and the rest of them down the line. In previous years farmers in the west could rely upon the cattle market. A farmer could take a few steers into the market when he could not sell his grain. For the past few years our farmers have been able to get a fine return for their cattle, but during the last two years the price of cattle has been reduced at least 50 per cent and the return to the farmer is much less than he needs to meet all his payments or even to make any substantial payment on his debt.
The real seriousness of the situation is just beginning to be felt. October, November and December are the farmer's pay days. He is usually able to deliver 10 or 15 bushels per seeded acre, get advances and meet his obligations. He was able to keep in operation in that way.


But taxes are going up. Gasoline, oil, fertilizer, hail insurance, repair bills are all items which have increased tremendously in the last few years. What is causing more concern is the fact that with navigation on the lakes due to close, with the congestion of grain in the terminal and local elevators, with the boats tied up at the wharves being1 filled with wheat, any movement of wheat from the west seems to be almost an impossibility. Everybody knows that throughout the winter months there will be no appreciable movement of wheat. The farmer is going to have to wait until next spring at least before enough wheat will move to permit him to deliver even ten bushels of wheat per seeded acre, let alone 15 bushels for his total acreage. When will he get payment for the wheat grown in 1953? That is what is causing grave concern.
The fact that Great Britain did not sign the international wheat agreement this year leaves the western wheat grower quite disturbed about the future. When we had the five-year wheat agreements the western wheat grower had an assurance of security. But that is now gone. The farmer today is critical of those who were responsible for failing to maintain an effective wheat agreement.
For many years this group urged the government to maintain price controls and contended that the resultant high costs of production might place us in a position where the commodities which we have to export would be at such a figure that they would not be purchased in foreign markets. We contended that those countries might not be able to purchase our grain. In spite of our pleadings the government removed price controls. The fact is that those who did that, and allowed costs to rise so high are the ones who are responsible today for pricing us out of the wheat markets overseas.
In 1949, with price controls, the ordinary combine which a farmer used to harvest his wheat could be purchased for about $3,000. At that time a farmer could sell a good steer for as high as $250 and 12 steers would pay for his combine. Since 1949 when price controls were taken off the cost of farm machinery has been allowed to rise and today a self-propelled combine costs a farmer in the west $6,000 to bring home to his farm. When he takes a good steer to market to pay for that he finds that it will bring him only $100 and he now has to sell 60 steers to pay for the combine instead of 12. Twelve steers is the average yearly production of a mixed farmer in our area.
The Address-Mr. Castleden
A study of trade figures since 1946 as prepared by the dominion bureau of statistics shows a rather serious trend. Great Britain has been our traditional market and has always taken a large share of Canada's exports of wheat. Taking the period 1946 to 1952 inclusive, the figures of trade between Canada and Great Britain reveal the disturbing fact that in that seven-year period Great Britain bought about $2,480 million more of goods from Canada than Canada bought from Great Britain. That means a shortage of Canadian dollars in Great Britain with which to purchase Canadian wheat.
One would have naturally thought that it would be to Canada's interest to encourage the importation of goods from Great Britain in order to create a balance of trade and thus provide enough good Canadian dollars to buy our wheat. This would have gone a long way toward providing sufficient payment to the farmer for his wheat in order to cover the increased costs of production which this government has brought upon him.
In 1948 the government did encourage trade with Great Britain by suspending section 6 of the Canadian tariff act and encouraging British goods to come into Canada. Great Britain sent to this country small English cars worth many millions of dollars every year. They established contacts in this country and for a few years carried on an exceptionally fine trade. But in 1951 this government reimposed section 6 of the tariff act. This imposed terrific duties against British cars coming into this country and the result was, according to the dominion bureau of statistics, that for the last half of 1951, Great Britain exported to this country only about 14 per cent of the number of cars which she had sent in the first half of 1951.
In regard to the United States, however, what do we find? The Canadian balance of trade with the United States during the same period, 1946-1952, showed the reverse to be true. Canada bought from the United States the sum of $3,313 million more in goods than the United States bought from us.
There are Canadian dollars in the United States but unfortunately the United States is in the same market. The United States competes with us in world markets with agricultural products. The whole effect of the government action has been to place us in a position of dependence on the United States for markets which ordinarily could have been found in Great Britain, and it has placed overseas markets in the position where they cannot buy our goods. Western farmers know this. The people who study
502	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Castleden the wheat business, and there are people who are watching these trends with a great deal of concern, know that the welfare of the west depends on our ability to sell our wheat at least at the cost of production plus a little more for the farmer's work. They hold this government responsible, first, for allowing costs to increase and, secondly, for losing much of our export market.
Personally, with the situation facing us in the west today and with no international markets, I would advise every farmer in the west to get out of debt as quickly as he possibly can.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare

speechtext: The farmers were never more free of debt than they are now under this government.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
They are still in debt and the figures will prove it. If the present situation continues when the farmer is not allowed to deliver even three bushels of wheat they will have to go to the banks to borrow money to carry on and they will have to carry on while they are even more in debt.
The farmer knows the situation and he is watching it very carefully. He is worse off than his neighbour across the border in the United States.
The United States department of agriculture undertook a program under which they arranged cash advances for grain properly stored on the farm. The farmer there knows when he plants seed in the ground in the spring and starts to raise cattle that there is going to be a minimum price. If the same situation existed in western Canada as existed in the United States there would be provision for payment to the farmer for grain properly stored on the farm. The United States department of agriculture send their grain buyers, qualified men, down to inspect the grain on the farmers' farms. The inspector grades it, inspects it and where it is properly stored places a seal on it and makes the farmer an initial payment against future delivery. The same thing can be done here. It should be done here.
If the government wished to. prevent the farmers getting into debt they could institute a similar policy in the west today. Otherwise the farmers in the west will be compelled to go very heavily into debt. It is time the government realized that trade is most important to the farmers. It is the foundation of their success or failure. Their prosperity depends on trade and they expect this house to make some suggestions as to what should be done in the way of encouraging that trade. We should be encouraging trade between Canada and any other country willing to trade with us, first by eliminating


restrictions against goods as much as possible; second, accepting sterling where necessary or desirable for Canadian products; third, encouraging even barter where necessary and where feasible; and relaxing trade on non-military goods with all countries, in cases where we can possibly trade with them.
We should also institute a two-price system on Canadian agricultural products; first, a parity price based on costs within Canada for that portion sold on our domestic market, and secondly, the best price obtainable for producers on export sales, something similar to what is presently in operation in the Canadian wheat board for No. II class of wheat and wheat needed for home consumption.
Then we should have producers groups marketing their own products through marketing boards to be given required assistance by way of federal or complementary legislation and adequate floor price support through the Agricultural Prices Support Act to include cereal grains as well as other commodities.
That, we think, is the least the government can do in dealing with the agricultural economic situation facing those who have sent us here from the west to speak for them.
With the largest surplus of grain probably in the history of this country now before us, Canada has also a great opportunity to feed the hungry people of the world. At the present time there should be storage provided for the grain on western farms which is now in open storage. The latest figures published on November 15 reveal, from a survey of the situation, that there are at the present time some 58 million bushels of grain out in open storage in the prairie provinces. If that grain is not moved by spring, melting snow and rain that come in the spring may ruin it. Surely the government is responsible to some extent to see that that grain is not lost with so many hungry people in the world. If it were lost it would be a tragedy.
The storage problem in this country has not been met. Nor have steps been taken to keep pace with our capacity to produce. Production should be a good, not a bad thing. Farmers are storing their own grain. They have got their bins full, their garages full and even the chicken coops are full. They are not being paid for storing it and I think they should be, but this government should at least see that if there is extra grain there should be facilities for storing it. I would recommend to the government the immediate construction of some 20 storage elevators to take care of the surplus, and they could build them out in the prairie, where they are

immune from attack, and spread them in places throughout the country where long hauls would be avoided. Two such elevators could be placed at such points as Yorkton and Canora, both on a direct railway route to the port of Churchill. Within my own constituency there are excellent places for building such storage elevators similar to those which exist at Saskatoon and Moose Jaw. We have the facilities there and the railroads run east and west to Winnipeg, and we are fortunate also in being on the main C.N.R. feeder line through Hudson Bay Junction to Fort Churchill. I am sure that suitable land in that vicinity would be made available. The Saskatchewan Power Corporation could provide them with a good reliable supply of power, and other service facilities there are of the very best.
There is another matter of tremendous importance to the grain growers in the west which is causing them considerable concern and that is the future of our wheat board. They are aware that the Minister of Trade and Commerce is not a strong advocate of government enterprise. They are alert also for any signs which could threaten the board's existence or efficiency. The fight of the western producer over the last 40 years has been a struggle to release himself from the clutches of those who previously robbed him through the manipulation of the Winnipeg grain exchange. Through those 40 years he has built himself up a large co-operative elevator system. In our province alone there are something over 1,100 co-operatively owned elevators. There are also the pool terminal elevators at the head of the lakes. They are ready to carry on the facilities for handling grain. They have their own flour mill and their own oil extracting mill built by the farmers themselves on a co-operative basis so that by handling all the grain through their own companies they could share in any gains or in any profits which might be made. But just as valuable as that to them is the establishment in this country of a wheat board to which they undertook to deliver all their wheat. The government wheat board sells that grain on the best market possible and returns to the farmer the full results of the sale less the cost of handling. No middlemen are allowed to come in there to depress the market, where they buy the grain from the farmer and boost it up when they come to sell it and pocket the difference. The wheat board is the one bulwark which the farmers of the west hold. It is the thing that saves them from the exploitation of the grain exchange, and they want to keep it.
However, the farmers find that they are not allowed to deliver the grain to their own
The Address-Mr. Castleden elevators. The allocation of cars throughout the past four or five years has been of such a nature that the farmer is not permitted to deliver to his own elevator because they do not supply them with cars. The farmer frequently comes and finds there are no cars supplied to his own elevator and he has to turn it over to the line elevator company which has been his opposition and has exploited him for many years. The recent action of the transport controller in suspending the operation of the car order book without even the courtesy of consultation or a request for the opinion of the wheat pools or the farm organizations has caused deep resentment among the farmers. It has added to their fears that the best interests of the farmer and his organizations are not being served by the Canadian wheat board in some important instances. Something is seriously wrong when any producer is compelled to deliver his grain to his own opposition. The car order book was one means whereby he was assured that he could deliver his grain to the elevator of his own choice.
The third thing about this wheat board which has been causing deep resentment, because we are afraid for its future, is the appointment of the assistant manager of one of the line elevator companies to the Canadian wheat board. The western farmers have been asking for the past three years for producer representation through one of the commissioners on that board. They consider this recent appointment as a slap in the face.
The line elevator companies are the natural opponents of the co-operative pools. They are the natural opponents of the principles of orderly marketing. With such appointments being made, we wonder about the future effectiveness of the board against exploitation. I should like to assure the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) right here and now that the grain growers of the prairies have a deep and abiding determination to hold onto that one bulwark they have which protects them against exploitation. They gained this board through 40 years of struggle, and they are going to hang onto it. It is the foundation of their security. We will never return to the grain exchange.
The farmers have formed a union out in the west. They are making a request that when they voluntarily ask the wheat board to make deductions for union dues from their payments for grain, the wheat board will be empowered to make those deductions. That is not an entire check-off but it is a case where there is a voluntary request on the part of the grain grower himself. The farmers are willing to pay for the cost.

The Address-Mr. Castleden
In the livestock industry today there exists a situation similar to that which existed for many years with regard to grain. Some three or four large packing firms control the price of cattle to the farmer and, indirectly, the price of meat to the consumer. It is almost a complete parallel with what used to happen with regard to grain in the grain exchange. There is no standard of grading. There is nothing upon which we can base a fair price. The farmer is at the complete mercy of these buyers who come up there in the stockyards. I have stood in the stockyards and watched them. The cattle are not government graded at any price. I have watched those cattle come in-ranging from cutters and canners to finished stall-fed steers. I have seen canner cows selling for as low as 3 cents a pound; for good steers, some selling as low as 9 cents a pound, and some of the better ones perhaps at 14 cents. They are absolutely at the mercy of the buyers. But still, on going to the butcher shop we find no corresponding decline in the price of meat to the consumer.
One irate farmer came to me after having his cattle thus stolen from him. He went down from there to the butcher shop, and then he came over to see me. He said, "Can you tell me what the trouble is? Why is it that every time the price of steers goes down, the price of meat goes up?" He said, "You fellows have to pay plenty for it. Why can I not get something out of it? Something is terribly wrong."
I believe the representative from the province of Quebec who was in the recent dominion-provincial agricultural conference stated something similar when he said this: "You know, there is a warble fly which destroys the good leather on the hide of a cow, and after years of research we have found an insecticide which will take care of that insect. But there is some kind of insect that somehow changes the price of meat from the time we sell it to the time it gets into the butcher shop." He said, "If we could ever find that insect that causes the price to go from 4 and 5 cents up to 65 and 85 cents, we would be doing a great deal of good to . the farmer."
When the farmer ships his cattle directly to the packing company he is entirely at their mercy with regard to grade, weight and price. Surely a board could be established which would see that grading of these cattle is properly done in order to prevent the farmer from having the stuff stolen from him, as it is today. Surely something can be done similar to what is done with regard to selling wheat in whatever market it can be sold at the highest price, returning to the


farmer everything that is received for the meat less the cost of handling. I believe the packing companies should do their work. I think they should be paid for doing their work and also that they should pay the labour working in their plants a decent wage. But I do not think that they should have the right to handle that price to suit themselves and to take out of the consumer and the producer the tremendous profits which have been revealed by such companies as Canada Packers. I do not think that should be permitted, and I do not think that any government which permits this thing to continue can expect long to have the support and the respect of the Canadian people.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I am going to urge something which has been urged by this group for many years. It is something that was urged by its former leader, the late Mr. J. S. Woodsworth. It is a thing that has been repeatedly urged by our leader, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, and other members of this group. We want to draw the attention of the Canadian people to this fact and we are sent down here to do so. So long as there are two-thirds of the people in this world hungry, we should be willing to share with those countries some of the super-abundance which we have. Two-thirds of the people in this world are ill-fed, ill-clothed and ill-housed.
There never was a time in the world when we needed the good will of people throughout the world as much as we need it today. The western continent today is choked1 with food. Surely it would be better to share this food and our surpluses with hungry people and to win their good will than it would be to frighten them with an iron fist. Surely the hand of friendship is better than the mailed fist. Surely Canada will take the lead and speed up the sending of this food to hungry people. If we can spend billions of dollars in time of war, surely we can spend a few hundred millions to see that these distressed people are fed. Surely we can extend enough good will so they will see the inherent goodness that lies within the Canadian people. It should be an expression from the Canadian people which would have the support of everyone. I doubt if there is one member in the house who would vote against the granting of a few million dollars to help to build good' will among the peoples of the world. The opportunity exists today. I do not know how long it will exist but it must be seized now if it is to be seized at all. If we fail to meet the challenge before us today then history will hold us responsible.

I took part, personally, in that debate, and I appreciate the fact that that bill was introduced. What I was speaking about, however, was the standard cairn heretofore erected. In this country, with our granite, our marble, our slate and all the other things which can be used in erecting monuments, I would hope these conventional standardized things would not be used again along the highways.
I do not wish to sound unduly critical, but I would make reference to the bronze plaques which have been placed on those cairns. I do not think we can afford to have a uniform, dull standard with respect to those plaques. As I understand it, in the early days of this country-and I have had some personal experience with this matter-at Grand Pre there was what was known as the massacre of Colonel Noble and his men. I, in company with other citizens, got the old historic sites and monuments board to have a cairn erected. The cairn, to which I have referred, was erected, but there appeared on it uniform wording in French and English, commenting upon the heroism shown by those gallant soldiers of the French and British armies who fell on that occasion. Well, there were no members of the French army who fell on that occasion. As all the men who died in Colonel Noble's army were scalped in their drawers, it was rather hard to see the necessity for this uniformity.
We all realize that in this country there are a variety of antecedents, but principally the two great races from which we have come; and out of that amalgam has grown this nation. But that does not mean that every time we turn around we have to render obeisance the one to the other. I am sure there are places in the province of Quebec where memorials should be erected, but without reference to something which Englishmen may have done there; and in [DOT]other parts of Canada memorials should be erected without necessarily referring to the French.

We do not need dull uniformity in those matters; we have got past that in our national development. I am offering this as a matter of modified criticism. I do not wish anyone to think I do not appreciate the work this historic sites and monuments board has done; but I do believe the time has come when we should embark upon a wider basis than we have used heretofore, and that we should have properly marked those places and events which have been ignored too much in the past.
Having spoken about the recognition of the dead, I should like to make some passing references in recognition of the living. I was rather surprised to find the other day- and I am sure other hon. members were surprised too-that the O.B.E., the C.B.E. and the M.B.E. orders, which at one time were awarded to civilians, have now been reserved exclusively for those in the armed forces. I find there are no awards whatsoever in this country for any civilian contributions to the state or the nation.
I do not think that is right. I am not criticizing the fact that these awards are given to military personnel. While they have their own service decorations for valour, if it is advisable to have these awards conferred upon them, well and good. However, when we were at war the C.B.E. and the M.B.E. were awarded to various civilians. I am told now that this was done on the theory that they had made valuable contributions to our war effort. Those decorations were, as one might say, first cousins once removed to those given to military personnel. That custom, however, has been discontinued.
This subject comes to my mind because my attention was called to an old lady in Halifax who for 40 years had worked as a voluntary port worker, meeting ships and immigrants, serving tea and coffee, spending her own money on their behalf and giving freely of her spare time-often more than her spare time-to that work. During the last war the work in that area became so heavy that the authorities had to have fully paid help to do it. She became too old for the work with the result that she had to leave, and since that time has been working in a sailors' mission in Halifax.
I suggest that that lady has made a great contribution to the lives of seamen and immigrants from other countries in the world. That is the type of person I have in mind to whom some recognition should be given. I am not thinking of knighthoods, or awards of that kind, but there are those who contribute in a social or humanitarian way to the life of the nation. We talk about the Canadian
The Address-Mr. Nowlan flag we should have; we talk about a Canadian national anthem and these other earmarks of Canadian autonomy. I think as a nation we should also have recognition for those who make contributions to it. As a matter of fact we know that universities give degrees. Learned societies create fellows, and some churches confer recognition in some ways. But the only recognition we have here of a public nature is that which is conferred upon those gentlemen and ladies who sometimes are presented in the other place. And that, I may say, is a very reserved list at the moment, and one not entirely available to the general public.
So I do say that in my opinion, for whatever it is worth, I believe the time has come when civilian awards of some kind should be made. I would hope that during the lifetime of this parliament-and I do not mean this session, but rather this parliament-in some way and by some non-partisan procedure we as responsible members of the House of Commons representing the people of Canada could by some means give recognition which would express our appreciation for lives well spent and jobs well done.
One matter in this potpourri, to which I referred before, is grants to universities in this country. I am not going to develop any lengthy arguments, because most hon. members are conversant with this subject. However, in the Massey report a recommendation was made that the federal treasury grant to each province the sum of 50 cents per head of population, this money to be divided among the students attending universities in those various provinces. This provision has been in force for some three years, I believe, and undoubtedly has done a great deal of good.
I worked out some figures the other evening, and while my ability as a mathematician is not such as to warrant my receiving one of these awards I mentioned a moment ago, I believe my figures are reasonably accurate. They indicate a spread between the universities in the various provinces extending from $459 per student attending a university in Newfoundland to various other sums in other provinces. I am willing to admit that there is only one university in Newfoundland, and that is one reason for this very large figure. From the $459 per student in Newfoundland the figure drops to $205 per student attending university in Prince Edward Island, and down through $180 and $165 for other provinces until we finally reach the figure of $95 per student attending university in Nova Scotia.
I realize that this is a difficult problem, and yet I am convinced that it cannot be so

I believe that in the circumstances they have fulfilled their function in a masterly fashion and I wish to congratulate them. I congratulate them especially for having given proof of their remarkable bilingualism. In doing so, they have shown that the younger generation is aware of the importance of a dual culture.
The hon. member for Roberval has shown that even in a part of the country which is remote from Ontario and the maritime provinces French-Canadians make it their duty to learn English, in order to better understand the mentality of their English-speaking brothers. As for the member for York Centre who, at the age of 23, did not know a single word of French, he has shown very elegantly that, with a determined will, it is possible to solve all difficulties and I congratulate him. He has asked me to speak to him in French only, which I shall gladly do.
I therefore rejoice at this state of mind which will help improve national unity based upon mutual respect and understanding among all Canadians.

Some time ago the New York Times was introducing new Canadian correspondents, 
and it referred to Tania Long, in private life Mrs. Raymond Daniell, as follows:
When the war started, she and her mother went to Sweden. Swedish was the first language she learned. After the war, she returned to Berlin. There she learned German and, at home, Russian.

Is it not marvellous that the one person can speak Swedish, German, Russian, French and English fluently? Is it not sufficient to make us think of the great superiority we would have if all Canadians could speak the two official languages of this country?

It will come one day. It may be far away in the point of view of an individual, but in the life of a nation time does not count. On that day all prejudices will fade away and Canada will find unity in diversity, with no one having to sacrifice one iota of his national characteristics.
At times people have blamed the province of Quebec for taking controversial stands, but I ask every Anglo-Canadian not to judge us harshly. You must understand our history and the battles we have had to fight to maintain our national heritage. It is only with time that the wounds inflicted in the past will disappear. France, which was invaded three times by Germany since 1870, is careful in accepting the co-operation of the new Germany. This is quite understandable.
The same thing can be said about the French Canadians. But as France is indicating a willingness to collaborate with the allies in creating a new Germany, so are French Canadians giving their full cooperation toward our national life.
